s1loc: Bootle sits inside Sefton's busy voluntary scene, where FareShare Merseyside redistributes surplus food to more than 200 charities and community groups across the borough and Wirral with the help of around 100 volunteers. South Sefton Foodbank works in the Trussell network through local churches, while Volunteer Centre Sefton recruits Community Champions across Bootle, Litherland, Waterloo and Netherton. The Salvation Army runs a long-standing presence on Stanley Road, and grassroots projects such as Netherton Community Gardens give residents a hands-on way to help neighbours.

The sector here runs at every size. National charities with shops on Stanley Road lean on trade accounts and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects in Linacre, Orrell and the L30 estate work on a shoestring. The L30 Community Centre, run by Fun 4 Kidz, shows how tiny outfits stretch every pound. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group.

Beyond food, Bootle's charitable life spreads through hospice and carer support that reaches across south Sefton. Sefton Carers Centre backs unpaid carers in Bootle and the wider district, and hospice charity shops dot Stanley Road and the local parades alongside the Salvation Army store. Mutual-aid and wellbeing work runs out of the Netherton Family Wellbeing Centre, and faith groups across Linacre, Orrell and Seaforth keep collection points and warm-space sessions going through winter. These named projects, many volunteer-led, form the backbone of everyday community support in the town.

s1loc: Harrogate's voluntary sector is anchored by Harrogate District Foodbank, a Trussell-network charity that handed out more than 11,000kg of emergency food across the district in early 2024 with around 70 volunteers giving their time. Harrogate and District Community Action runs the local volunteering directory and connects residents to dozens of groups, while Harrogate Hospital and Community Charity recruits ward and fundraising volunteers. Saint Michael's Hospice underpins much of the town's giving, raising funds through care for local families across the district.

The sector runs at every size here. Regional and national charities with shops and central buying sit alongside small community groups working hand to mouth. Saint Michael's Hospice runs around 11 preloved shops across Harrogate, Ripon, Knaresborough and Boroughbridge, while the foodbank, parish pantries and volunteer-run projects in Bilton, Starbeck and Jennyfield stretch every donation. We are set up to serve the regional charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the larger names and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest volunteer group.

Harrogate's wider charitable life takes in named shops on King's Road, Cold Bath Road and Ripon Road, including the Saint Michael's House and Home furniture store, plus Cancer Research and other high-street charity outlets in the town centre. The hospital charity supports chaplaincy, cancer services and outpatient clinics through volunteers, and community action work reaches mutual-aid and warm-space groups in Bilton, Starbeck and the surrounding villages. From hospice retail to grassroots support circles, named projects across these neighbourhoods keep Harrogate's everyday giving running.

s1loc: Maidenhead's voluntary scene centres on Maidenhead FoodShare, a charity that supports around 200 people a week and, after 15 years, finally has a permanent home on Reform Road. It works alongside Windsor Foodshare and draws surplus stock through FareShare South West, which distributes food to scores of food banks and community groups. The RBWM Together network ties local food and essentials support together, while Thames Hospice, based on Windsor Road in Maidenhead, raises money through care for families across the borough.

Thames Hospice fields specialist shops, including a vintage and retro boutique, and FoodShare's new base adds a community cafe for people facing homelessness, young families and those facing isolation. Charity shops cluster through the town centre and out to Cookham, and mutual-aid and warm-space groups in Boyn Hill, Cox Green and Furze Platt keep neighbourly support going.
